# Book III, Proposition 27

*Angles standing on equal circumferences are equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> In equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it, in our measure of circumferences · Euclid's argument, with one step changed

<p align="center"><em>Turn III.26 round: in the equal circles ABC, DEF, stand angles on the equal circumferences BC, EF (red), and they come out equal, at the centres G, H (yellow) and at the circumferences, at A and D (blue).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/27.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.27, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For in equal circles ABC, DEF, on equal circumferences BC, EF, let the angles BGC, EHF stand at the centres G, H, and the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences;

I say that the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF,

and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

For, if the angle BGC is unequal to the angle EHF,

one of them is greater.

Let the angle BGC be greater; and on the straight line BG, and at the point G on it, let the angle BGK be constructed equal to the angle EHF. [I. 23]

Now equal angles stand on equal circumferences, when they are at the centres; [III. 26]

therefore the circumference BK is equal to the circumference EF.

But EF is equal to BC;

therefore BK is also equal to BC, the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore the angle BGC is not unequal to the angle EHF;

therefore it is equal to it.

And the angle at A is half of the angle BGC,

and the angle at D half of the angle EHF; [III. 20]

therefore the angle at A is also equal to the angle at D.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

| | |
|---|---|
| Proof | ✅ Proved |
| Statement | The whole enunciation. Angles at the circumferences of any size, and at the centres where they stand on BC; since our measure carries no radius, it holds in any two circles. |
| Argument | Euclid's, with one step changed. Euclid's reductio for the angles at the centres, and his halving by III.20 where the angles at the circumferences are acute; where they are right or obtuse, the Lean halves the measure of the circumference instead (`Circumference.standing`). |
| Representation | "In equal circles" is kept from Euclid, and the proof uses it through III.26 as he does; but the circumferences are measured by angles, so the statement would hold without it. The centres G and H are given, as the enunciation speaks of angles at the centres. |
| Reviewed | The statement and the argument read against Heath's text, for every departure from Euclid, at commit [`66e9871`](https://github.com/jackChallis/stoicheia/commit/66e9871) ([the record](../../review/III/27.toml)) |

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop27.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop27.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they
stand at the centres or at the circumferences. -/
theorem Prop27 {A B C D E F G H : Point} {ABC DEF : Circle} (hcircles : EqualCircles ABC DEF)
    (hG : Centre G ABC) (hH : Centre H DEF) (hA : OnCircle A ABC) (hB : OnCircle B ABC)
    (hC : OnCircle C ABC) (hD : OnCircle D DEF) (hE : OnCircle E DEF)
    (hF : OnCircle F DEF) (hBAC : Triangle B A C) (hEDF : Triangle E D F)
    (heq : standing ABC B A C = standing DEF E D F) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F ∧
      (SameSideOf G A B C → SameSideOf H D E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F) := by
  -- For in equal circles ABC, DEF, on equal circumferences BC, EF, let the angles BGC, EHF
  -- stand at the centres G, H, and the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences;
  -- I say that the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF,
  -- and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.
  have centres : SameSideOf G A B C → SameSideOf H D E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F := by
    intro hGA hHD
    /- We name the circumferences BC, EF by points Q, R beyond them, across BC from A and
       across EF from D; the centres lie on the sides of A and D. -/
    obtain ⟨Q, hQA, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hBAC.acb []
    obtain ⟨R, hRD, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hEDF.acb []
    have hBC : circumference ABC B Q C = circumference DEF E R F := by
      rw [← standing_eq_circumference hQA.symm, ← standing_eq_circumference hRD.symm]
      exact heq
    have hGQ : OppositeSidesOf G Q B C := hGA.trans_opposite hQA.symm
    have hHR : OppositeSidesOf H R E F := hHD.trans_opposite hRD.symm
    -- For, if the angle BGC is unequal to the angle EHF,
    -- one of them is greater.
    /- Either circle may have the greater angle. As in I.26, we write the reductio once and
       use it with the circles named either way round. -/
    have greater : ∀ {B C E F G H Q R : Point} {ABC DEF : Circle}, EqualCircles ABC DEF →
        Centre G ABC → Centre H DEF → OnCircle B ABC → OnCircle C ABC → OnCircle E DEF →
        OnCircle F DEF → OppositeSidesOf G Q B C → OppositeSidesOf H R E F →
        circumference ABC B Q C = circumference DEF E R F → ∠ E H F < ∠ B G C → False := by
      intro B C E F G H Q R ABC DEF hcircles hG hH hB hC hE hF hGQ hHR hBC hlt
      -- Let the angle BGC be greater; and on the straight line BG, and at the point G on it, let
      -- the angle BGK be constructed equal to the angle EHF. [I. 23]
      have hGB : G ≠ B := (ne_of_centre_of_on hG hB).symm
      obtain ⟨K', B', hB', hK'C, hK'GB'⟩ := BookI.Prop23 hGB hHR.triangle.acb hGQ.triangle.cab
      /- I.23 gives only the direction of GK. We take K on that ray at the distance GB
         from G, and System E, Diagram-segment 3, puts it on the given circle. -/
      have hK'G : K' ≠ G := hK'C.triangle.ne₁₃.symm
      obtain ⟨K, hK_ray, hGK⟩ := OnRay.exists_len_eq hGB hK'G.symm
      have hK : OnCircle K ABC := on_circle_of_len_eq hG hB hGK
      have hBGK : ∠ B G K = ∠ E H F := by
        rw [angle_onRay_right hK_ray hGB.symm, ← angle_onRay_left hB' hK'G]
        exact (angle_symm hB'.2.1 hK'G).trans hK'GB'
      have hGBK : Triangle G B K := (SameSideOf.of_onRay hK_ray hK'C).triangle
      -- Now equal angles stand on equal circumferences, when they are at the centres; [III. 26]
      /- For III.26 we name the circumference BK by a point P beyond it, and take a point of
         each circle on the centre's side. -/
      obtain ⟨P, hPG, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hGBK.bca []
      obtain ⟨X, hX, hXG⟩ := Prop2.sameSide ⟨G, hG⟩ hB hK hGBK.bca
      obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYH⟩ := Prop2.sameSide ⟨H, hH⟩ hE hF hHR.triangle
      -- therefore the circumference BK is equal to the circumference EF.
      have hBK : circumference ABC B P K = circumference DEF E R F :=
        (Prop26 hcircles hG hH hX hB hK hY hE hF (hXG.trans_opposite hPG.symm)
          (hYH.trans_opposite hHR)).1 hPG.symm hHR hBGK
      -- But EF is equal to BC;
      have hEF_BC := hBC.symm
      -- therefore BK is also equal to BC, the less to the greater: which is impossible.
      have h := hBK.trans hEF_BC
      rw [Circumference.centre hG hB hK hPG.symm, Circumference.centre hG hB hC hGQ,
        hBGK] at h
      rw [h] at hlt
      exact lt_irrefl _ hlt
    -- Therefore the angle BGC is not unequal to the angle EHF;
    -- therefore it is equal to it.
    rcases lt_trichotomy (∠ B G C) (∠ E H F) with h | h | h
    · exact (greater hcircles.symm hH hG hE hF hB hC hHR hGQ hBC.symm h).elim
    · exact h
    · exact (greater hcircles hG hH hB hC hE hF hGQ hHR hBC h).elim
  have hAD : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
    by_cases hGH : SameSideOf G A B C ∧ SameSideOf H D E F
    rotate_left
    · /- Our statement also covers right and obtuse angles at the circumference,
         where no angle at the centre in Euclid's sense stands on the same
         circumference. There the circumference is twice the angle standing on it
         (`Circumference.standing`), and halves of equal things are equal. -/
      rw [Circumference.standing ⟨G, hG⟩ hA hB hC hBAC.acb,
        Circumference.standing ⟨H, hH⟩ hD hE hF hEDF.acb] at heq
      exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq heq
    -- And the angle at A is half of the angle BGC,
    have h20A := Prop20 hG hA hB hC hGH.1
    -- and the angle at D half of the angle EHF; [III. 20]
    have h20D := Prop20 hH hD hE hF hGH.2
    -- therefore the angle at A is also equal to the angle at D.
    exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq
      (h20A.symm.trans ((centres hGH.1 hGH.2).trans h20D))
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hAD, centres⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L55): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L62) (through [`angle_onRay_left`](../../Elements/Figure/Angles.lean#L40) and [`angle_onRay_right`](../../Elements/Figure/Angles.lean#L47)): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle ABC is the triangle ACB. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L34): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L22): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L38): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`on_circle_of_len_eq`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L30) (used here): A point at the distance of the radius from the centre is on the circle. (Diagram-segment 3, the half that Definition 15 doesn't give)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L50): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (through [`Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Areas.lean#L52)): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45) (through [`Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Areas.lean#L52)): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (used here): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (through [`Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Areas.lean#L52)): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (used here): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**A circumference equal to its own part.** Euclid argues by *reductio ad absurdum*. Were the angle BGC greater than EHF, the angle BGK made equal to EHF within it would stand, by III.26, on a circumference BK equal to EF, and so to BC: the less equal to the greater. Our figure draws the impossible case, with BGC the greater, so that K has somewhere to fall.

**The converse inherits the cases.** Heath writes: "This proposition is the converse of the preceding one, and the remarks about the method of treating the different cases apply here also" (vol. 2, p. 59). Among those remarks, under III.26, is Dionysius Lardner's way with a right or obtuse angle: bisect it, and work with the halves. Euclid's last step halves the angles at the centres by III.20, which works only when the angles at the circumference are acute. Our statement still asks for every size, since IV.11 needs obtuse angles, and our proof reaches them through our measure of circumferences.

**Where does K fall?** I.23 gives the angle BGK, but not where its side GK meets the circumference. We take GK equal to the radius GB, and System E, Diagram-segment 3, puts K on the circle (`on_circle_of_len_eq`). The measure then turns Euclid's impossibility back into angles: BK equal to BC would make the less angle BGK equal to the greater, BGC.

**The modern way.** A rigid motion of the plane carries any arc onto any arc of the same length in a circle of the same radius, and keeps every angle, so equal arcs subtend equal angles at the centres and, since the angles in one segment are all equal, at the circumferences too. It is not Euclid's route, which runs through III.26.

## Further reading

- For the motions behind the modern way, which carry an arc onto any equal arc, Jacques Hadamard's [*Lessons in Geometry, I: Plane Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1090/mbk/057) (2008), Book II, ch. VI, "On the Motion of Figures" (p. 99) (also on [III.13](13.md)).
- For the rigid motions of the modern way, Felix Klein's ["A comparative review of recent researches in geometry"](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3161) (1893, free online), his Erlangen Programme of 1872, in which a geometry is known by the motions it allows.
